## Introduction



## Data exploration
First, we want to see the structure of our data. What variables do we have, for which countries, etc. 
Then we will check if the data has any empty, missing or weird entries.
Lastly, we will give some Rshiny tools so you can explore the data yourself. 

### Data structure
**What columns do we have? How many rows?**
```{r}
colnames(Life_Expectancy_Data)

paste(nrow(Life_Expectancy_Data), "rows")
```
There are 21 columns and 2864 rows. 
Important to note for some columns:  
* Hepatitis B, Measles, Polio and Diphteria show % of *vaccination* coverage, not incidence  
Further information on what these columns represent is explained on the Kaggle page under Data sources:  
[Kaggle data sources](https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/lashagoch/life-expectancy-who-updated/data).

**How are the rows structured?**

For example, how many countries are there? How many years?  
And do these explain the number of rows seen?
```{r}
row_explain = c(Countries = 0, Years = 0, Product = 0, Nrows = nrow(Life_Expectancy_Data))
row_explain["Countries"] = length(unique(Life_Expectancy_Data$Country))
row_explain["Years"] = length(unique(Life_Expectancy_Data$Year))
row_explain["Product"] = row_explain["Countries"] * row_explain["Years"]
row_explain
```
As you can see, this seems to indicate that all 179 countries occur for all 16 years to explain the 2864 rows in the dataset.  

Which specific years are included?
```{r}
years = unique(Life_Expectancy_Data$Year)
years = years[order(years)]
years
```
So from 2000 to 2015  


However, we will further validate this structure:  
How many countries are present 16 times, so once for each year?
```{r}
sum(table(Life_Expectancy_Data$Country) == 16)
```
This all seems right, so the years and countries are used consistently! 


**What data types are present?**
```{r column info}
str(Life_Expectancy_Data)
```
The Economy status developing column contains only ones and zeros, so True and False. 
It is the inverse of the developed column.  
The Country and Region columns contain characters, where Region has 9 possibilies. 
All other columns are integers or numeric. 

**What is the life expectancy distribution?**
```{r}
boxplot(Life_Expectancy_Data[Life_Expectancy_Data$Year == 2000 & Life_Expectancy_Data$Economy_status_Developing == T,"Life_expectancy"],
        Life_Expectancy_Data[Life_Expectancy_Data$Year == 2000 & Life_Expectancy_Data$Economy_status_Developing == F,"Life_expectancy"],
        Life_Expectancy_Data[Life_Expectancy_Data$Year == 2015 & Life_Expectancy_Data$Economy_status_Developing == T,"Life_expectancy"],
        Life_Expectancy_Data[Life_Expectancy_Data$Year == 2015 & Life_Expectancy_Data$Economy_status_Developing == F,"Life_expectancy"],
        main = "Life expectancy distribution \n Between developed and developing countries for 2000 and 2015",
        names = c("Developing\n 2000", "Developed\n 2000", "Developing\n 2015", "Developed\n 2015"),
        col = c("salmon", "turquoise"),
        ylab = "Life expectancy (years)",
        ylim = c(30,90))
```


**How many countries are either developed or developing?**
Do any developing countries change into developed countries over the years?
```{r row info} 
develop = c(Developed = 0, Developing =  0, Total = 0)
develop["Developed"] = sum(Life_Expectancy_Data$Economy_status_Developed == T) / 16
develop["Developing"] = sum(Life_Expectancy_Data$Economy_status_Developed == F) / 16
develop["Total"] = develop[1] + develop[2]
develop

data %>% filter(Year %in% c(2000, 2015)) %>% group_by(Country) %>% summarise(n = n_distinct(Economy_status_Developed)) %>% filter(n > 1)

```
The countries do not switch from developing to developed, they stay in the same category

**Which five countries have the highest life expectancy and which 5 the lowest, for each year?**
```{r}
Life_Expectancy_Data %>%
  group_by(Year) %>%
  slice_max(Life_expectancy, n = 5, with_ties = FALSE) %>%
  ungroup()

Life_Expectancy_Data %>%
  group_by(Year) %>%
  slice_min(Life_expectancy, n = 5, with_ties = FALSE) %>%
  ungroup()
```

**Are there empty values or NA values?**
```{r data info}
empty = c(Empty = 0, NAs = 0)
# how many NAs?
empty["NAs"] = sum(is.na(Life_Expectancy_Data))
empty["Empty"] = sum(Life_Expectancy_Data == "")
empty
```
All together, we now understand the data structure and have seen that it is complete. It is important to keep in mind that each country occurs 16 times, once for each year. 

### Visualisation
**Here we will make a shiny application that easily lets the user explore life expectancy over time for a selected country. **

```{r}
ui = page_sidebar(
  title = "Life expectancy over time",
  sidebar = sidebar(
    "This graph allows you to select any country in the dataset and then plot
    its life expectancy over time",
    selectInput("country", "Select a country", choices = unique(Life_Expectancy_Data$Country))
  ),
  card(
    card_header("Life expectancy over time plot"),
    plotOutput("plot")
  )
)

server = function(input, output){
  output$plot = renderPlot({
    x = Life_Expectancy_Data[Life_Expectancy_Data$Country == input$country, "Year"]
    y = Life_Expectancy_Data[Life_Expectancy_Data$Country == input$country, "Life_expectancy"]
    plot(
      x,y,
      main = paste("Life expectancy over time for", input$country),
      xlab = "Time (years)",
      ylab = "Life expectancy"
    )
  })
}

shinyApp(ui, server)

```

**Here we will make an interactive table using Rshiny**
```{r}
ui = page_sidebar(
  title = "Interactive Life expectancy table",
  sidebar = sidebar(
    "Here you can interactively inspect the WHO Life Expectancy data"
  ),
  card(
    card_header("WHO Life Expectancy data"),
    DT::dataTableOutput("table")
  )
)

server = function(input,output){
  output$table = DT::renderDataTable(DT::datatable({
    data = Life_Expectancy_Data
    data
  }))
}

shinyApp(ui, server)
```


## Analysis Wietske 

```{r}
Life_expectancyModel <- lm(
  Life_expectancy ~ Schooling + Infant_deaths + Under_five_deaths + GDP_per_capita + Hepatitis_B + Measles + Population_mln +
    Thinness_ten_nineteen_years +
    Thinness_five_nine_years +
    Adult_mortality + Incidents_HIV +
    BMI + Alcohol_consumption +
    Polio + Diphtheria + Economy_status_Developed,
  data = Life_Expectancy_Data
)

Life_expectancyModel

summary(Life_expectancyModel)

```

These results showed that de model explained 97.92 % of the variation in life expectancy (R² = 0.9792). Several predictors showed significant associations with life expectancy (p < 0.05). For example, Adult mortality and under-five deaths had negative associations, while schooling and GDP per capita showed positive associations. 

##standardized model - Beta values (β)

```{r}
standardizedFullModel <- lm(
  scale(Life_expectancy) ~
    scale(Schooling) +
    scale(Infant_deaths) +
    scale(Under_five_deaths) +
    scale(GDP_per_capita) +
    scale(Hepatitis_B) +
    scale(Measles) +
    scale(Population_mln) +
    scale(Thinness_ten_nineteen_years) +
    scale(Thinness_five_nine_years) +
    scale(Adult_mortality) +
    scale(Incidents_HIV) +
    scale(BMI) +
    scale(Alcohol_consumption) +
    scale(Polio) +
    scale(Diphtheria) +
    scale(Economy_status_Developed),
  data = Life_Expectancy_Data
)

summary(standardizedFullModel)


```

Standardization allows the relative strength of the predictors to be compared because all variables are expressed in standard deviations. Adult mortality (β = −0.590) showed the strongest negative association with life expectancy, followed by under-five deaths (β = −0.266) and infant deaths (β = −0.140). GDP per capita showed the strongest positive association (β = 0.046). The model explained 97.92% of the variation in life expectancy (R² = 0.9792).

##Checking for multicollinearity 

```{r}
library(car)
vif(standardizedFullModel)

reducedModel <- lm(
  Life_expectancy ~ Schooling + Under_five_deaths +
    GDP_per_capita + Hepatitis_B + Measles +
    Population_mln + Thinness_ten_nineteen_years +
    Adult_mortality + Incidents_HIV + BMI +
    Alcohol_consumption + Diphtheria +
    Economy_status_Developed,
  data = Life_Expectancy_Data
)
vif(reducedModel)

```

The initial model showed signs of multicollinearity, particularly for infant deaths (VIF = 44.76), under-five deaths (VIF = 45.29), polio (VIF = 12.01) and diphtheria (VIF = 13.00). To reduce multicollinearity, infant deaths, polio and thinness among children aged 5–9 years were removed from the model. In the reduced model, VIF values decreased substantially, with no variables exceeding 10. However, under-five deaths (VIF = 7.93) and adult mortality (VIF = 7.80) still showed relatively high VIF values, indicating that some multicollinearity remained.


##final standardized model 

```{r}

standardizedReducedModel <- lm(
  scale(Life_expectancy) ~
    scale(Schooling) +
    scale(Under_five_deaths) +
    scale(GDP_per_capita) +
    scale(Hepatitis_B) +
    scale(Measles) +
    scale(Population_mln) +
    scale(Thinness_ten_nineteen_years) +
    scale(Adult_mortality) +
    scale(Incidents_HIV) +
    scale(BMI) +
    scale(Alcohol_consumption) +
    scale(Diphtheria) +
    scale(Economy_status_Developed),
  data = Life_Expectancy_Data
)

summary(standardizedReducedModel)


```

The standardized reduced model allows comparison of the relative strength of the remaining predictors. Adult mortality (β = −0.595) showed the strongest negative association with life expectancy, followed by under-five deaths (β = −0.394). GDP per capita (β = +0.050) showed the strongest positive association. The model explained 97.87% of the variation in life expectancy (R² = 0.9787), with most predictors showing statistically significant associations (p < 0.05).


##visualisation 

```{r}

library(ggplot2)
library(tidyr)
library(patchwork) 

p1 <- ggplot(Life_Expectancy_Data,
       aes(Adult_mortality, Life_expectancy)) +
  geom_point(size = 0.4) +
  geom_smooth(color = 'red', method = "lm", se = TRUE) +
  labs(x = "Adult mortality",
       y = "Life expectancy",
       title = "Adult mortality and life expectancy")
p1



p2 <- ggplot(Life_Expectancy_Data,
       aes(Under_five_deaths, Life_expectancy)) +
  geom_point(size = 0.4) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = TRUE) +
  labs(x = "Under-five deaths",
       y = "Life expectancy",
       title = "Under-five deaths and life expectancy")
p2

p3 <- ggplot(Life_Expectancy_Data,
       aes(GDP_per_capita, Life_expectancy)) +
  geom_point(size = 0.4) +
  geom_smooth(color = 'green', method = "lm", se = TRUE) +
  labs(x = "GDP per capita",
       y = "Life expectancy",
       title = "GDP per capita and life expectancy")
p3

combinedplot <- p1/ p2/ p3 
combinedplot


```

The three strongest predictors in the standardized reduced model were adult mortality, under-five deaths and GDP per capita. The plots show the relationship between each predictor and life expectancy. Adult mortality and under-five deaths show negative relationships with life expectancy, whereas GDP per capita shows a positive relationship. These are individual relationships, whereas the regression coefficients represent associations while controlling for the other variables.



```{r}

beta_data <- data.frame(
  Variable = c(
    "Adult mortality",
    "Under-five deaths",
    "GDP per capita",
    "BMI",
    "Alcohol consumption",
    "Developed economy",
    "Schooling",
    "HIV incidence",
    "Thinness (10-19 years)",
    "Hepatitis B",
    "Diphtheria",
    "Measles",
    "Population"
  ),
  Beta = c(
    -0.5947, -0.3943, 0.05010, -0.03451,
    0.03168, 0.03120, 0.03193, 0.02786,
    -0.01706, -0.009361, 0.003362,
    0.004135, -0.002360
  )
)

ggplot(beta_data, aes(x = reorder(Variable, Beta), y = Beta)) +
  geom_col() +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(
    x = "Variable",
    y = "Standardized beta coefficient",
    title = "Standardized regression coefficients"
  ) +
  theme_bw()

```



```{r}
ggplot(beta_data,
       aes(reorder(Variable, abs(Beta)), abs(Beta))) +
  geom_col() +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(
    x = "Variable",
    y = "Absolute standardized beta",
    title = "Ranking of variables by association strength"
  ) + theme_bw()
```


##final plot with remaining significant associations 

```{r}

Beta_data_significant <- data.frame(
  Variable = c(
    "Adult mortality",
    "Under-five deaths",
    "GDP per capita",
    "BMI",
    "Alcohol consumption",
    "Developed economy",
    "Schooling",
    "HIV incidence",
    "Thinness (10-19 years)",
    "Hepatitis B"
  ),
  Beta = c(
    -0.5947, -0.3943, 0.05010, -0.03451,
    0.03168, 0.03120, 0.03193, 0.02786,
    -0.01706, -0.009361
  )
)

ggplot(Beta_data_significant,
       aes(reorder(Variable, abs(Beta)), Beta,
           fill = Beta < 0)) +
  geom_col() +
  coord_flip() +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c("TRUE" = "red", "FALSE" = "green"),
    labels = c("TRUE" = "Negative", "FALSE" = "Positive")
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Variable",
    y = "Standardized beta (β)",
    title = "Standardized regression coefficients",
    fill = "Association"
  ) +
  theme_bw()


```

To compare the relative importance of each predictor, standardized regression coefficients were calculated. Variables were visualized using horizontal bar charts ordered by effect size. A final subset containing only statistically significant associations was visualized with color coding to distinguish between positive (green) and negative (red) relationships. 




##Box plots for the strongest determinants 
Using the results from the analysis above, here we visualise the differences in the three determinants with the strongest correlation to life expectancy between 2000 and 2015 in box plots. Then outliers are explored, the biggest ones will be investigated further.
```{r}

diff.both <- data %>% 
  filter(Year %in% c(2000, 2015)) %>%
  arrange(Country, Year) %>%
  group_by(Country, Economy_status_Developed) %>%
  filter(n() == 2) %>%
  summarise(across(c(GDP_per_capita, Adult_mortality, Under_five_deaths), 
                   ~ (last(.x) - first(.x)) / first(.x) * 100),
            .groups = "drop") %>%
  mutate(Economy = factor(Economy_status_Developed,
                          levels = c(0, 1),
                          labels = c("Developing", "Developed"))) %>%
  pivot_longer(c(GDP_per_capita, Adult_mortality, Under_five_deaths),
               names_to = "variable", values_to = "diff.both")

ggplot(diff.both, aes(x = Economy, y = diff.both, fill = Economy)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  facet_wrap(~ variable, scales = "free_y",
             labeller = labeller(variable = c(
               GDP_per_capita  = "GDP per capita",
               Adult_mortality = "Adult mortality",
               Under_five_deaths = "Under five deaths"))) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Change from 2000 to 2015 (%)") +
  theme_light()+
  theme(legend.position = "none")

#Finding the outliers    
data %>%
  filter(Year %in% c(2000, 2015)) %>%
  select(Country, Economy_status_Developed, Year, GDP_per_capita) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = Year, values_from = GDP_per_capita) %>% 
  mutate(diff.both = (`2015` - `2000`) / `2000` * 100) %>%
  group_by(Economy_status_Developed) %>%
  slice_max(diff.both, n = 5, with_ties = FALSE) %>%
  ungroup()

data %>%
  filter(Year %in% c(2000, 2015)) %>%
  select(Country, Economy_status_Developed, Year, Adult_mortality) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = Year, values_from = Adult_mortality) %>%
  mutate(diff.both = (`2015` - `2000`) / `2000` * 100) %>%
  group_by(Economy_status_Developed) %>%
  slice_max(diff.both, n = 5, with_ties = FALSE) %>%
  ungroup()

data %>%
  filter(Year %in% c(2000, 2015)) %>%
  select(Country, Economy_status_Developed, Year, Under_five_deaths) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = Year, values_from = Under_five_deaths) %>%
  mutate(diff.both = (`2015` - `2000`) / `2000` * 100) %>%
  group_by(Economy_status_Developed) %>%
  slice_max(diff.both, n = 5, with_ties = FALSE) %>%
  ungroup()

```
So Eritrea was an outlier in GDP data and Syria was an outlier in both Adult mortality and Under five deaths data.

## **Linde's Kladblok**

### Shiny app

```{r}


# Prepare data
map_data <- Life_Expectancy_Data %>%
  mutate(
    iso3 = countrycode(Country,
                       origin = "country.name",
                       destination = "iso3c")
  )

# Available indicators
indicators <- c(
  "Life_expectancy",
  "Infant_deaths",
  "Under_five_deaths",
  "Adult_mortality",
  "Alcohol_consumption",
  "BMI",
  "GDP_per_capita",
  "Schooling",
  "Hepatitis_B",
  "Polio",
  "Diphtheria",
  "Incidents_HIV",
  "Population_mln",
  "Thinness_ten_nineteen_years",
  "Thinness_five_nine_years",
  "Economy_status_Developed",
  "Economy_status_Developing"
)

# Shiny UI
ui <- fluidPage(
  titlePanel("Life Expectancy Data"),
  sidebarLayout(
    sidebarPanel(
      h4("Data selection"),
      sliderInput(
        "year",
        "Select year:",
        min = min(map_data$Year),
        max = max(map_data$Year),
        value = max(map_data$Year),
        step = 1,
        sep = "",
        ticks = TRUE
      ),
      selectInput(
        "indicator",
        "Select indicator:",
        choices = indicators,
        selected = "Life_expectancy"
      ),
      selectInput(
        "color_by",
        "Colour scatterplot by:",
        choices = c(
          "Region" = "Region",
          "Development status" = "Development"
        ),
        selected = "Development"
      ),
      sliderInput(
        "population_size",
        "Minimum population size (mln):",
        min = min(map_data$Population_mln),
        max = 100,
        value = min(map_data$Population_mln),
        step = 1,
        sep = "",
        ticks = TRUE
      )),
    mainPanel(
      wellPanel(
        h3("Global distribution"),
        plotlyOutput("world_map", height = "600px")
      ),
      wellPanel(
        h3("Scatter plot"),
        plotlyOutput("scatter_plot", height = "500px"),
        h4("Correlation"),
        verbatimTextOutput("correlation")
      )
    )
  )
)

# Shiny server
server <- function(input, output) {
  filtered_data <- reactive({
    data <- map_data %>%
      filter(Year == as.numeric(input$year)) %>%
      filter(!is.na(iso3))
    if (length(input$population_size) > 0) {
      min_population <- min(as.numeric(input$population_size))
      data <- data %>%
        filter(Population_mln >= min_population)
    }
    data
  })
  # World map
  output$world_map <- renderPlotly({
    plot_data <- filtered_data()
    plot_ly(
      data = plot_data,
      type = "choropleth",
      locations = ~iso3,
      z = ~.data[[input$indicator]],
      text = ~paste(
        "Country:", Country,
        "<br>Year:", Year,
        "<br>", input$indicator, ":",
        .data[[input$indicator]],
        "<br>Population (mln):", Population_mln
      ),
      hoverinfo = "text",
      colorscale = "Viridis",
      colorbar = list(title = input$indicator)
    ) %>%
      layout(
        title = paste(
          input$indicator,
          "in",
          input$year
        ),
        geo = list(
          showframe = FALSE,
          showcoastlines = TRUE,
          projection = list(type = "natural earth")
        )
      )
  })
  # Scatterplot
  output$scatter_plot <- renderPlotly({
    plot_data <- filtered_data()
    selected_variable <- input$indicator
    plot_data$selected_indicator <- plot_data[[selected_variable]]
    # Choose colour grouping
    if (input$color_by == "Region") {
      plot_data$colour_group <- as.factor(plot_data$Region)
    } else {
      plot_data$colour_group <- ifelse(
        plot_data$Economy_status_Developed == 1, "Developed", "Developing")
    }
    model <- lm(
      Life_expectancy ~ selected_indicator,
      data = plot_data
    )
    plot_data$fitted_values <- fitted(model)
    plot_data <- plot_data %>%
      arrange(selected_indicator)
    plot_ly(
      data = plot_data,
      x = ~selected_indicator,
      y = ~Life_expectancy,
      type = "scatter",
      mode = "markers",
      color = ~colour_group,
      colors = if (input$color_by == "Development") {
        c("Developing" = "salmon", "Developed" = "turquoise")
      } else {
        "Set3"
      },
      text = ~paste(
        "Country:", Country,
        "<br>Year:", Year,
        "<br>", selected_variable, ":",
        selected_indicator,
        "<br>Life expectancy:", Life_expectancy,
        "<br>Population (mln):", Population_mln,
        "<br>Group:", colour_group
      ),
      hoverinfo = "text"
    ) %>%
      add_lines(
        data = plot_data,
        x = ~selected_indicator,
        y = ~fitted_values,
        inherit = FALSE,
        name = "Regression line",
        line = list(color = "darkgrey", width = 3)
      ) %>%
      layout(
        title = paste(
          selected_variable,
          "vs Life Expectancy in",
          input$year
        ),
        xaxis = list(title = selected_variable),
        yaxis = list(title = "Life Expectancy (years)"),
        legend = list(title = list(text = input$color_by))
      )
    
  })
  output$correlation <- renderText({
    
    plot_data <- filtered_data()
    selected_variable <- input$indicator
    
    x <- plot_data[[selected_variable]]
    y <- plot_data$Life_expectancy
    
    model <- lm(y ~ x)
    
    correlation <- cor(x, y, method = "pearson")
    r_squared <- summary(model)$r.squared
    p_value <- summary(model)$coefficients[2, 4]
    slope <- coef(model)[2]
    intercept <- coef(model)[1]
    n <- length(x)
    paste0(
      "\nPearson correlation (r): ", round(correlation, 3),
      "\nR-squared (R²): ", round(r_squared, 3),
      "\nP-value: ", format.pval(p_value, digits = 3),
      "\nSlope: ", round(slope, 3),
      "\nIntercept: ", round(intercept, 3),
      "\nNumber of countries (n): ", n
    )    
  })
  
}


# Run app
shinyApp(ui = ui, server = server)
```

### Nested dataset and correlation of variables with life expectancy in regions

```{r}
library(tidyverse)
library(purrr)
library(magrittr)
library(dplyr)
```

```{r}
LED_nested <- Life_Expectancy_Data |> group_by(Region) |>  nest()
LED_nested

mean(pluck(LED_nested, "data", 1)$Life_expectancy)

LED_nested <- LED_nested |>
  mutate(avg_lifeExp = map_dbl(data, ~ mean(.x$Life_expectancy)))

LED_nested <- LED_nested |>
  mutate(model = map(data, ~ lm(Life_expectancy ~ Population_mln + GDP_per_capita + Year, data = .x))) #you see how pop, gdp and year relate to life expectancy in each continetn

#Let's take along more predictors
LED_nested <- LED_nested |> mutate(model_extended = map(data,
                                                        ~ lm(
                                                          Life_expectancy ~ Population_mln +
                                                            GDP_per_capita +
                                                            Year +
                                                            Infant_deaths +
                                                            Under_five_deaths +
                                                            Adult_mortality +
                                                            Alcohol_consumption +
                                                            BMI +
                                                            Schooling +
                                                            Hepatitis_B +
                                                            Polio +
                                                            Diphtheria +
                                                            Incidents_HIV +
                                                            Thinness_ten_nineteen_years +
                                                            Thinness_five_nine_years,
                                                          data = .x
                                                        )
))

LED_nested |> pluck("model_extended", 1)

LED_nested %<>%  mutate(prediction = map2(model, data, function(.lm, .data) predict(.lm, .data)))
LED_nested %<>% mutate(correlation = map2_dbl(data, prediction, function(.data, .prediction) cor(.data$Life_expectancy, .prediction)))
LED_nested

LED_nested %<>%  mutate(prediction_extended = map2(model_extended, data, function(.lm, .data) predict(.lm, .data)))
LED_nested %<>% mutate(correlation_extended = map2_dbl(data, prediction_extended, function(.data, .prediction_extended) cor(.data$Life_expectancy, .prediction_extended)))
LED_nested
```


This shows that only the variables taken along in assignment of day 5, the prediction of the Life expectancy fits poorly. However, if we do take more variables available to try to fit the r\^2 as high as possible, the fit is much better. This shows the concept, but isn't mathematically feasible. Therefore, we should aim to find the variables that are most of influence on the life expectancy to answer our research question. (This answer will be answered by Wietske.)

### Correlation of variables in developed/developing countries with Life Expectancy

**What is the difference between the correlation of variables in developed and developing countries on the Life Expectancy?**

Lets make an object of the means over all the years first so we can work with that

```{r}
country_means <- Life_Expectancy_Data %>% group_by(Country, Region) %>% summarise(across(2:19,~ mean(.x)), .groups = "drop")

correlation_by_economy <- country_means %>%
  group_by(Economy_status_Developed) %>%
  group_modify(~ {
    numeric_data <- .x %>%
      select(where(is.numeric))
    cor_matrix <- cor(
      numeric_data,
      use = "pairwise.complete.obs"
    )
    data.frame(
      Variable = rownames(cor_matrix),
      Correlation = cor_matrix[, "Life_expectancy"]
    ) %>%
      filter(Variable != "Life_expectancy")
    
  }) %>%
  ungroup()
```

```{r}
correlation_by_economy <- country_means %>%
  group_by(Economy_status_Developed) %>%
  group_modify(~ {
    variables <- .x %>%
      select(where(is.numeric)) %>%
      names() %>%
      setdiff("Life_expectancy")
    bind_rows(lapply(variables, function(v) {
      pair <- .x %>%
        select(all_of(c(v, "Life_expectancy"))) 
      
      # Check that the correlation can be calculated
      if (nrow(pair) < 3 ||
          sd(pair[[v]]) == 0 ||
          sd(pair$Life_expectancy) == 0) {
        
        return(tibble(
          Variable = v,
          Correlation = NA_real_,
          p_value = NA_real_,
          n = nrow(pair)
        ))
      }
      
      test <- cor.test(
        pair[[v]],
        pair$Life_expectancy,
        method = "pearson"
      )
      
      tibble(
        Variable = v,
        Correlation = unname(test$estimate),
        p_value = test$p.value,
        n = nrow(pair)
      )
    }))
  }) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  mutate(
    Significance = case_when(
      p_value < 0.001 ~ "***",
      p_value < 0.01  ~ "**",
      p_value < 0.05  ~ "*",
      TRUE ~ ""
    )
  )

correlation_by_economy <- correlation_by_economy %>%
  group_by(Economy_status_Developed) %>%
  mutate(
    adjusted_p = p.adjust(p_value, method = "BH"),
    Significance_adjusted = case_when(
      adjusted_p < 0.001 ~ "***",
      adjusted_p < 0.01  ~ "**",
      adjusted_p < 0.05  ~ "*",
      TRUE ~ ""
    )
  ) %>%
  ungroup()

plot_develop_sig <- ggplot(correlation_by_economy,
                           aes(x = reorder(Variable, Correlation),
                               y = Correlation,
                               fill = factor(Economy_status_Developed, levels = c(0, 1),
                                             labels = c("Developing", "Developed")))) +
  geom_col() +
  geom_text(
    aes(
      y = Correlation + ifelse(Correlation >= 0, 0.04, -0.04),
      label = Significance_adjusted
    ),
    size = 4
  ) +
  coord_flip() +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  facet_wrap(~ Economy_status_Developed, labeller = as_labeller(c(
    "0" = "Developing",
    "1" = "Developed"
  ))) +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c(
      "Developing" = "salmon",
      "Developed" = "turquoise"
    )
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Correlation of variables with life expectancy",
    subtitle = "Statistical significance of Pearson correlations",
    x = "Variable",
    y = "Pearson correlation coefficient"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

plot_develop_sig

correlation_by_economy %>%
  arrange(Economy_status_Developed, p_value) %>%
  select(Economy_status_Developed, Variable, Correlation, p_value, n, Significance_adjusted)
```

Likely won't use it, but let's do it per region as well:

```{r}
correlation_by_region <- country_means %>%
  group_by(Region) %>%
  group_modify(~ {
    
    variables <- .x %>%
      select(where(is.numeric)) %>%
      names() %>%
      setdiff("Life_expectancy")
    
    bind_rows(lapply(variables, function(v) {
      
      pair <- .x %>%
        select(all_of(c(v, "Life_expectancy"))) %>%
        drop_na()
      
      # Check that the correlation can be calculated
      if (nrow(pair) < 3 ||
          sd(pair[[v]]) == 0 ||
          sd(pair$Life_expectancy) == 0) {
        
        return(tibble(
          Variable = v,
          Correlation = NA_real_,
          p_value = NA_real_,
          n = nrow(pair)
        ))
      }
      
      test <- cor.test(
        pair[[v]],
        pair$Life_expectancy,
        method = "pearson"
      )
      
      tibble(
        Variable = v,
        Correlation = unname(test$estimate),
        p_value = test$p.value,
        n = nrow(pair)
      )
    }))
  }) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  mutate(
    Significance = case_when(
      p_value < 0.001 ~ "***",
```
